title: Effects of photovoltaic panels on soil temperature and moisture in desert areas
abstract: Photovoltaic power generation is an important clean energy alternative to fossil fuels. To reduce CO2 emissions, the Chinese government has ordered the construction of a large number of photovoltaic (PV) panels to generate power in the past two decades; many are located in desert areas because of the sufficient light conditions. Large-scale PV construction in desert areas can alter the local microclimate and soil conditions, thereby affecting the growth of vegetation. However, few studies have focused on the effects of PV panels on the environment of desert areas. In this study, we investigated the effects of PV panels on soil moisture and temperature via a whole-year field experiment at a PV power plant in a desert area in western China. The in situ soil moisture and temperature at a depth of 0–0.4 m were measured under three types of PV shading conditions: shaded by fixed-tilt (FIX) PV panels, shaded by oblique single-axis (OSA) PV panels, and no shading. The results showed that the soil temperature and moisture at sites under PV shading were significantly affected compared with those at sites without shading. PV panels increased the average soil temperature during winter but decreased it during the other three seasons. Moreover, the warming effect of FIX PV panels on the soil is more apparent than that of OSA PV panels. PV panels have positive effects on soil moisture. Compared with that at the sites without shaded areas, the average soil moisture under the FIX PV panels and under the OSA PV panels increased by 14.7% and by 11.1%, respectively. These data provide support for future studies on vegetation restoration around PV power plants in desert areas.

## RESEARCH ARTICLE

## Effects of photovoltaic panels on soil temperature and moisture in desert areas

Shengjuan Yue[1,2,3] & Mengjing Guo[1] & Penghui Zou[4] & Wei Wu[1] & Xiaode Zhou[1]

> Received: 27 August 2020 /Accepted: 17 November 2020 / Published online: 5 January 2021 # Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2021

## Abstract

Photovoltaic power generation is an important clean energy alternative to fossil fuels. To reduce CO2 emissions, the Chinese government has ordered the construction of a large number of photovoltaic (PV) panels to generate power in the past two decades; many are located in desert areas because of the sufficient light conditions. Large-scale PV construction in desert areas can alter the local microclimate and soil conditions, thereby affecting the growth of vegetation. However, few studies have focused on the effects of PV panels on the environment of desert areas. In this study, we investigated the effects of PV panels on soil moisture and temperature via a whole-year field experiment at a PV power plant in a desert area in western China. The in situ – soil moisture and temperature at a depth of 0 0.4 m were measured under three types of PV shading conditions: shaded by fixedtilt (FIX) PV panels, shaded by oblique single-axis (OSA) PV panels, and no shading. The results showed that the soil temperature and moisture at sites under PV shading were significantly affected compared with those at sites without shading. PV panels increased the average soil temperature during winter but decreased it during the other three seasons. Moreover, the warming effect of FIX PV panels on the soil is more apparent than that of OSA PV panels. PV panels have positive effects on soil moisture. Compared with that at the sites without shaded areas, the average soil moisture under the FIX PV panels and under the OSA PV panels increased by 14.7% and by 11.1%, respectively. These data provide support for future studies on vegetation restoration around PV power plants in desert areas.

Keywords PV panels[. ] Desert areas[. ] Soil temperature[. ] Soil moisture[. ] Field observations

## Introduction

The development of renewable energy sources has become the primary solution to alleviating global warming and the energy crisis (Panwar et al. 2011). According to the International Energy Agency (IEA) Sustainable

Development Scenario, renewable power capacity is expected to expand by 50% between 2019 and 2024, and this increase is led by the use of solar photovoltaic (PV) energy (IEA 2019). Solar PV energy is one of the most promising emerging renewable technologies. The total installed capacity worldwide exceeded 510 GW in 2019, and the installed capacity will reach 4600 GW by 2050, which could prevent the emissions of up to 4 Gt of CO2 annually (IEA 2014).

The deployment of PV modules affects the photosynthetically active radiation and radiative flux balance, reduces the surface albedo, and alters the distribution of precipitation (Li et al. 2018b). These changes have a great impact on the driving factors of the local microclimate of spatial and temporal scale, such as evaporation, wind speed, air temperature, soil moisture, and soil temperature (Armstrong et al. 2014). In the UK, the installation of a grassland PV power plant altered the microclimate compared with that of an area without PV panels, and the PV arrays decreased the summer soil temperature by 5.2 °C and increased the winter soil temperature by 1.7 °C (Armstrong et al. 2016). At the same experimental site,

the mean soil temperature under the PV panels during the growing season was cooler by approximately 4 °C compared with that of the gap area between PV panel rows (Makaronidou 2020). In desert areas, the daily range of soil temperature at a depth of 5–10 cm at a solar farm was lower than that in areas without the PV farm (Yang et al. 2017). PV panels have different impacts on soil temperature in different climate zones. In the arid zone, the soil temperature under PV panels was 3.1 °C cooler than that of the control, and in the equatorial and temperate zones, it was 1.1 °C cooler. In addition, the soil under PV panels was cooler regardless of the seasonal changes at each region across the warm zones (Makaronidou 2020). Soil temperature is strongly correlated with soil moisture (Abu-Hamdeh 2003) because precipitation and evaporation regulate soil temperature via feedback on soil moisture content. Under PV panels, the soil moisture is greater, and the water-use efficiency is significantly improved (the efficiency increased by 328%) (Adeh et al. 2018). Similarly, the soil moisture content in the growing season was greater under PV panels and similar or only slightly different relative to the gap area outside of the growing season. The greater amount of soil moisture under the panels can promote vegetation growth (Makaronidou 2020). Specifically, under rainfall conditions, PV panels concentrate rainfall along the lower edge, thus causing a heterogeneous spatial distribution of soil moisture. Soil moisture heterogeneity may have an important impact on plant growth, especially in arid areas because small variations in water availability could have large effects on plant growth (D’Odorico et al. 2007). At a PV power plant in an arid area, the vegetation coverage increased from 13.4% under natural conditions to 90.5% in the 2 years after PV power plant construction (Liu et al. 2019). The vegetation restoration process at PV power plants creates positive conditions that help prevent desertification relatively quickly. Furthermore, the values of various ecosystem services at PV power plants have increased by more than 20 times (Liu et al. 2020). The above studies indicate that changes in soil temperature and moisture at PV power plants may have significant effects on ecosystem processes, including vegetation morphology, carbon cycling, and evapotranspiration rates (Dupraz et al. 2011). Therefore, more research is urgently needed to understand the effects of PV panels on soil temperature and moisture as well as their relationships.

In this study, the effects of different types of fixed-tilt (FIX) PV panels and oblique single-axis (OSA) PV panels on soil temperature and moisture in the Gonghe desert area of Qinghai Province were analyzed. The variation in soil temper– ature and moisture (0 0.4 m) under different types of panels and in non-PV areas were monitored in situ from January to December 2019. The objectives of this study were to (1) quantify the impact of different types of PV panels on soil moisture under a desert climate, (2) evaluate the effect of PV panels on soil temperature in different seasons and at different depths,

and (3) explore how PV panels affect soil temperature and moisture.

## Material and method

## Site description

Measurements were performed at the Gonghe PV power plant (36. 130° N, 100.574° E), Qinghai Province, which is located approximately 18 km south of Gonghe County (Fig. 1a). The study area has an elevation of 2900–3100 m, and the local climate is a typical alpine arid desert, with an annual average temperature of 4.1 °C. The annual average precipitation is 246.3 mm, and 90.4% of the annual precipitation is concentrated from May to September; moreover, the evaporation reaches 1716.7 mm, which is 6 times the precipitation (Zhao and Na 1996). The local soil parent material is loess or gravel, and the texture comprises mostly sandy loam and light silt loam (Shao et al. 1988). The main plant species are shallow-rooted ones, such as Achnatherum splendens, Leymus chinensis, and fringed sagebrush (Wei and Wu 2011).

## Instruments and experimental design

Different types of PV panels are installed in the study area. The FIX PV panels are tilted 34° from the horizontal plane and pointed towards the south, and the distance between the panels is approximately 7.5 m (Chang et al. 2018). The OSA PV panels are controlled by an automatic optical tracking system and can rotate in an east-west direction. A micrometeorological station (Fig. 1b, c, 36.131° N, 100.567° E, 2913 m) was constructed in the open space at the boundary of the FIX PV panels and the OSA PV panels, and it can measure air temperature, rainfall, air humidity, and wind speed. Three soil temperature and moisture monitoring sites were set up (Fig. 2a), and the installation depths of the monitoring sites were 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4 m. One monitoring site was located under a FIX PV panel (FIX site) and fully covered by the PV panel. Another monitoring site was located under an OSA PV panel (OSA site) and partially covered by the PV panel. The reference monitoring site (REF site) was located in an open space approximately 20 m from the PV panels, and it was not covered by a PV panel. The data from the REF site (i.e., non-PV) were compared with those from the other two sites. The vegetation under different types of PV panels and without PV panels area are shown in Fig. 2 b, c, and d. Detailed procedures for soil temperature and moisture monitoring experiments are provided in Fig. 3.

Fig. 1 a Location of the Gonghe PV power plant in Qinghai Province. b Micrometeorological station at the Gonghe PV power plant in Google Earth. c Image of a micrometeorological station on site

The following measurements were performed: (1) soil temperature and moisture were measured at depths of 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4 m using a Hydra Probe sensor (Campbell Scientific, Inc., USA); (2) air temperature was measured at 2.5 m above ground using an HMP155A sensor; and (3) rainfall was monitored with a TE525MM automatic recording rain gauge. All sensors were connected with a CR1000X data logger and powered by a solar cell. The parameters were measured automatically every 60 s, and the mean values were stored in 30-min tables. The measurements were continuously performed for 365 days from January 1 to December 31, 2019.

## Data analysis

The annual average, seasonal average, and diurnal average soil temperature and moisture values were calculated by averaging the original 30 min of data for comparison. A one-way analysis of variance, Pearson correlation analysis, and significance analysis were used to study the differences in soil temperature and moisture at the three monitoring sites, and each was performed using SPSS software (SPSS 22.0, SPSS, Inc., USA). Significant differences were determined at a significance level of 0.05. The figures were plotted using Origin software (OriginPro, OriginLab, USA).

## Results

## Analysis of soil temperature

## Annual change in soil temperature

The average soil temperature of three layers at each site was consistent with the trend of air temperature changes during the monitored period (January to December 2019) (Fig. 4). The average annual soil temperatures of the FIX, OSA, and REF sites were 5.7, 6.0, and 7.2 °C, respectively.

According to the soil temperature differences between the areas under PV panels and the area without PV panels (Fig. 5),

Fig. 4 Average soil temperature at depths of 0.1 to 0.4 m under the PV panels (FIX site and OSA site) and non-PV panel (REF site) and their response to air temperature (Tair)

the effect of the FIX PV panels on soil temperature throughout the year could be divided into two periods: from March to October (average air temperature 9.0 °C), the FIX PV panels had a cooling effect on soil temperature, with maximum decreases of 7.2 °C, 7.5 °C, and 6.5 °C at depths of 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4 m, respectively, and from November to February (average air temperature − 7.5 °C), the FIX PV panels had a warming effect on soil temperature, with maximum increases of 4.6 °C, 4.5 °C, and 2.8 °C at depths of 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4 m, respectively. The analysis of PV panel effects on soil temperature showed that a greater effect occurred on the surface layer than on the deep layer.

Notably, the OSA PV panel had a cooling effect on soil temperature most of the time. The maximum values decreased by 4.1 °C, 5.8 °C, and 4.7 °C at depths of 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4 m, respectively. A warming effect was observed only for the period from November to December, and the range of maximum increase was within 2.0 °C. Figure 5 also shows that the effect of FIX PV panels on soil temperature was significantly greater than that of OSA PV panels.

In terms of the annual average soil temperature, the PV panels (FIX and OSA PV panels) had a cooling effect on the soil temperature of each layer (0.1 to 0.4 m). The soil temperature of the 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4-m layers of the OSA PV panel was 1.1 °C, 1.2 °C, and 1.4 °C lower than the corresponding soil temperatures of the non-PV area, respectively; additionally, under the FIX PV panel, the decrease in soil temperature of each layer was the same at 1.5 °C.

## Seasonal change in soil temperature

The PV panel types had a significant impact on soil temperature at the three monitoring sites in different seasons (Fig. 6). In the spring, the REF site was significantly warmer than the OSA and FIX sites at depths from 0.1 to 0.4 m; at 0.1 m, the temperature at the REF site was 2.2 °C and 4.1 °C greater, respectively; at 0.2 m, the temperature at the REF site was 2.4 °C and 4.0 °C greater, respectively; and at 0.4 m, the temperature at the REF site was 2.2 °C and 3.5 °C greater, respectively. However, significant differences were not observed between the OSA and FIX sites at depths of 0.2 to 0.4 m (p > 0.05).

In summer, the soil temperature was significantly different among the three monitoring sites at all depths (p < 0.05), and the temperature decreased from the REF site to the OSA site and the FIX site. At 0.1 m, the temperature at the REF site was 1.5 °C and 4.0 °C greater than that at the OSA and FIX sites, respectively; at 0.2 m, the temperature was 1.9 °C and 4.0 °C greater than that at the OSA and FIX sites, respectively; and at 0.4 m, the temperature was 1.6 °C and 3.3 °C greater than that at the OSA and FIX sites, respectively.

## Vertical distribution of soil temperature

Figure 7 shows the vertical distribution of soil temperature. The soil temperature at these three monitoring sites increased with increasing depth in autumn and winter (Fig. 7c, d) but decreased with increasing depth in spring and summer (Fig. 7a, b). From spring to autumn, the soil temperature under the PV panels was lower than that in the areas without PV panels. In the summer, the soil temperatures at the OSA and FIX sites were 1.5–1.9 °C lower and 3.3–4.0 °C lower than that at the REF site, respectively, while in autumn, the soil temperature difference between the PV panel areas and the area without PV panels was very small. However, in winter, the soil temperatures at the OSA and FIX sites were 0.1–0.6 °C lower and 1.5–2.3 °C greater than that at the REF site, respectively.

## Analysis of soil moisture

## Annual change in soil moisture

The rainfall in the study area mainly occurs from May to September in summer and autumn, accounting for 80–90% of the annual rainfall. The winter and spring are considered dry seasons, with little rainfall.

The soil moisture at the three monitoring sites proved to be responsive to the local rainfall regime at the different depths (0.1 to 0.4 m) during the monitored period (January to December 2019) (Fig. 8).

The patterns of temporal variation in the soil moisture at different depths and at each monitoring site were similar. As the air temperature increased in the spring, the soil began to thaw, and the soil moisture in the shallow layer in the non-PV area increased sharply; however, in the freezing period in winter, the soil moisture decreased sharply and then maintained a stable value. In the wet season of summer and autumn, the soil moisture fluctuated with rainfall, and the fluctuation range was largest in the 0.1-m layer in the non-PV area; in contrast, owing to the shielding effect of the PV panels, the fluctuation

The soil moisture differences between the area under the PV panels and that without PV panel indicated that the PV panels increased soil moisture at depths of 0.1 to 0.4 m during the monitored period (except during the soil freezing period) (Fig. 9). The maximum soil moisture differences between the FIX PV and OSA PV areas and the non-PV area were 23.4%, 14.5%, and 14.2% and 17.6%, 9.2%, and 7.7%, respectively, at depths of 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4 m, respectively. Therefore, the soil humidification amplitude under the FIX PV panel was larger than that under the OSA PV panel.

In terms of the annual average soil moisture, PV panels had a humidifying effect. Compared with that of the non-PV area, the average soil moisture of the 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4-m layers of the OSA PV and FIX PV panel areas increased by 11.1%, 3.8%, and 1.3%, respectively, and 14.7%, 7.0%, and 6.6%, respectively.

## Vertical distribution of soil moisture

The vertical distribution of soil moisture in the 0.1 to 0.4-m profile in dry and rainy seasons was plotted on the basis of the field observation data from the three monitoring sites (Fig. 11). At depths of 0.1 to 0.4 m, the soil moisture in the dry and wet seasons was greatest at the FIX site and then the OSA site (except for 0.4-m depth in the dry season) and REF site.

For the non-PV area (REF site), soil moisture increased with depth (11.9% at 0.1 m and 15.6% at 0.4 m in the rainy season), and it was greater at the 0.4-m layer. However, under PV panels (FIX site and OSA site), the soil moisture first decreased and then increased with depth. In the rainy season, under the FIX and OSA PV panels, the soil moisture decreased from 30.8 to 23.3% and from 24.9 to 18.6%, respectively, and then increased to 26.5% and 19.3% in the 0.4-m layer, respectively.

The PV panels had a significantly greater effect on soil moisture in the rainy season than the dry season (Fig. 10). Significant differences were observed in soil moisture at depths of 0.1 to 0.4 m between the area under the PV panels and the non-PV area in the rainy season (p < 0.05), while no significant differences were observed in soil moisture at the 0.4-m layer between the area under the OSA PV panel and the non-PV area in the dry season (p > 0.05). ## Discussion

## Effects of PV panels on soil temperature

PV panels reduce incoming direct shortwave and outgoing longwave radiation fluxes from the soil below (Broadbent et al. 2019). These spatial variations in the radiative flux

balance directly affect the underground soil temperature, and obvious differences are observed in different climate regions and during different seasons. In the Qinghai Desert area, the effect of PV panels on soil temperature shows significant seasonal differences (Fig. 6). In autumn, PV panels have no significant effect on soil temperature. In the spring and summer, PV panels have a cooling effect. The FIX and OSA PV panels decreased the soil temperature by 4.0 °C and 1.5 °C at the 0.1m depth during summer, respectively. This change may be related to the PV panel-induced reduction in the amount of shortwave radiation reaching the ground (Weinstock and Appelbaum 2009). The soil temperature under the FIX PV panel was significantly lower than that under the OSA PV panel. This difference was because the OSA tracking PV panel receives more solar radiation than does the FIX PV panel and the solar radiation under the PV panel is more uniform (Valle et al. 2017).

In the winter, the FIX PV panel had a warming effect and increased the soil temperature by 2.3 °C. This increase may be attributed to the following reasons: (1) the lower solar altitude angle in winter reduces the amount of ground solar radiation (Weinstock and Appelbaum 2009); (2) the smaller sky angle under the PV panel reduces the net longwave radiation loss

Because the soil freezes in winter in the study area, the microbial and biological activities of the soil and litter were generally lower, and the difference in soil temperature had a limited effect on the plant-soil processes (Armstrong et al. 2016).

The decreasing soil temperature in summer and increasing soil temperature in winter under the PV panels alleviated the extreme cold and hot soil microenvironments in this desert area to a certain extent, which had a positive effect on improving the utilization rate of water and nutrients and the structure of the biological community (Belnap 1995). In terms of vegetation, excessive soil temperatures cause high temperature stress, inhibit chlorophyll synthesis (Xu and Huang 2000) and vegetation growth, reduce root biomass (Carón et al. 2015), slow root growth and vegetation regeneration (Nishar et al. 2017), and adversely affect vegetation regeneration (Althoff et al. 2016), thus affecting the whole life cycle of a plant (Walck et al. 2011). In addition, the increase in soil temperature can promote soil respiration (Dib et al. 2014) and increase the release of greenhouse gases such as CO2, which has a positive feedback effect on global warming (Bai et al. 2004).

## Effects of PV panels on soil moisture

The FIX PV panel increased the annual average soil moisture by 14.7% at the 0.1-m depth (the OSA PV panel increased by

11.1%). In the study area, the soil moisture in the dry season mainly comes from the release of frozen water, and it is largely affected by effect of soil temperature on the water evaporation intensity; however, the soil moisture in the wet season mainly depends on rainfall (Li et al. 2018a). The average soil moisture under the PV panels is similar to that in the non-PV area; however, the shield effect of the PV panels causes an uneven rainfall distribution (Elamri et al. 2018), which increases the local heterogeneity of the soil water distribution and creates more durable water storage under the PV panels (Adeh et al. 2018). Furthermore, the lower potential evapotranspiration under the PV panels is caused by the decrease in solar radiation, which leads to a decrease in dry-down, a decrease in the availability of soil water stores, and an increase in biomass, which also improves the water-use efficiency of vegetation and helps to prevent water loss in arid climate conditions (Adeh et al. 2018). PV power plants are usually located in arid and high potential evaporation areas, and vegetation growth in arid areas is affected by temperature (Beedlow et al. 2013) and available water (Zhou et al. 2011). When vegetation is under long-term drought stress, soil moisture will strongly control the spatiotemporal pattern of biomass (Kammann et al. 2011). In the context of global warming and water resource shortages, reducing water demand by shading plants could represent a consistent advantage in the near future (Wallace 2000).

The soil moisture under PV panels had a more significant humidification effect during the rainy season (vegetation growth period) (Fig. 10). The increase in soil moisture reduced the difference in soil temperature between day and

In arid sandy area, lower evaporation and greater soil moisture occur under PV panels, which provides more water for plant growth, thus promoting vegetation recovery and improving vegetation cover; for example, the vegetation coverage at a PV power plant reached 90.5% and effectively protected soil from wind erosion (Liu et al. 2019). In addition, the influence of vegetation change on the long-term climate of PV panels will affect carbon cycling at PV power plants (Armstrong et al. 2016). Soil moisture is also highly correlated with changes in microbial community structure and function (Brockett et al. 2012), which is an important driving force for overall microbial activity (Hackl et al. 2005). Changes in soil moisture under PV panels will further affect the PV power plant vegetation ecosystem nutrients and productivity, although its influence mechanism still needs further study.

Notably, the vertical distribution of soil moisture (Fig. 11) under the PV panels first decreases and then increases with depth, as observed in the 0.1-m layer for the high aquifer. This result may be attributed to the fact that PV panel shading results in lower evaporation intensity in shallow soil; thus, to improve the efficiency of PV panel power generation in desert areas, it is necessary to clean the PV panels regularly (Cui et al. 2017). The cleaning of underwater infiltration increases the shallow soil moisture content and provides additional water for vegetation growth under PV panels, which is beneficial for promoting the restoration of vegetation under PV panels.

## Conclusions

To provide more insight into the effects of PV panels on soil moisture and temperature, we conducted a monitoring experiment for soil moisture and temperature with or without PV panels in a desert area over a whole year. The following results were observed: (1) PV panels had a humidifying effect on soil moisture and the soil moisture had a significant difference in the rainy season, in which the annual average soil moisture of the FIX and OSA PV panel sites increased by 14.7% and 11.1%, respectively, at a depth of 0.1 m. (2) PV panels had a seasonal effect on soil temperature, with cooling effects from spring to autumn and warming effects during winter. In summer, the soil temperature of the FIX and OSA PV panel sites at a depth of 0.1 m decreased by 4.0 °C and 1.5 °C, respectively, whereas in winter, the soil temperature of the FIX PV panel site increased by 2.3 °C. (3) The cooling and humidification effects of FIX PV panels were greater than those of OSA PV panels. We concluded that the greater soil moisture and lower soil temperature under PV panels in summer were beneficial to ecosystem management and protection in desert areas. In the future, long-term in situ measurements should be performed and used to calibrate climate models.
